newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: U.N. council discussing statement on Iraqi flight.
newsitem.headline: U.N. council discussing statement on Iraqi flight.

text.p: The Security Council's Iraqi sanctions committee failed to reach consensus on Thursday on whether an Iraqi pilgrim flight to Saudi Arabia violated sanctions.
But council members said they were still working on a statement criticising Baghdad's action.
At issue is a flight on Wednesday from Baghdad to Jeddah and back taking 104 pilgrims on the annual haj.

Committee sources said the U.N. legal counsel, Under-Secretary-General Hans Corell of Sweden, told members during a closed door meeting that Gulf War resolutions barring Iraqi flights were not as clear cut as those imposed on Libya in 1992 in connection with the 1988 bombing of a Pan Am airliner over Lockerbie, Scotland.
But he was quoted as saying that, on the basis of past committee practise, Iraq did require advance permission for such flights.
Committee sources said Iraq had itself acknowleged this by requesting permission in the past, although the committee had refused to grant it.

Members of the council, which has the same 15-nation composition as the sanctions committee, said they were working on a statement that would make clear Iraq's obligation to obtain advance flight clearance on a case by case basis.

It would also remind other states of their obligations under the sanctions, which require denial of overflight permission for unauthorised Iraqi aircraft and the impounding of any that nonetheless landed in their territory.

A committee source said China and Guinea Bissau felt Iraq had not violated sanctions with its Baghdad-Jeddah-Baghdad flight, while the position of some other committee members was more ambiguous. The Security Council itself has the final word on any action.

American U.N. Ambassador Bill Richardson said on Thursday it was the United States' "firm view that Iraq proceeded with a violation of the sanctions ... For that reason we have taken the position that the Security Council should make a statement on this issue."
"We have made a lot of progress on language," he said, adding that the matter could be resolved on Friday.

Consensus among all members is required before the council can issue a statement. If consensus cannot be reached, the issue could be made the subject of a resolution and put to a vote, council sources said.
